title: We pay our way already: Data centres reject new tax
full_text:
Australia’s data centre industry has rejected calls for new taxes on the rapidly expanding sector, arguing it already pays its way, as the nation’s energy market operator revealed the artificial-intelligence boom is already reshaping electricity demand and driving a wave of new projects seeking to connect to the grid.
The Australian Energy Market Operator’s (AEMO) latest Quarterly Energy Dynamics report found data centres were helping change the pattern of electricity consumption across the National Electricity Market (NEM), offsetting lower demand caused by warmer weather and contributing to stronger electricity use during the middle of the day, despite continued growth in rooftop solar.
The findings come as the Albanese government seeks to attract billions of dollars of investment in artificial intelligence and data centres without leaving households to foot the bill for the additional generation, storage and transmission infrastructure needed to power them.
The Australian on Sunday revealed how some within Labor have advocated a levy on large data centres, underscoring growing debate within government over how the infrastructure needed to support the sector’s rapid expansion should be funded.
Data Centre Australia chief executive Belinda Dennett said the industry already paid its taxes, did not receive government incentives and privately funded the infrastructure it built, warning against policy settings that could undermine investor confidence.
“Data centre operators pay their taxes and neither receive nor ask for tax incentives. The investment in this critical enabling infrastructure is entirely privately funded,” she said.
Ms Dennett added that policy certainty is a key factor in investor confidence. “Australia is competing with markets in the region and globally that are intent on capturing the global infrastructure boom and with it the jobs, the supply chain investment and the ability to influence the governance of AI. Capital is mobile and investors have a choice.
“Australia is being presented with a once-in-a-generation opportunity to build future economic prosperity. But the window of opportunity is short and the landscape is very competitive.” AEMO’s latest assessment suggests the electricity demand associated with AI infrastructure is no longer a future challenge, but one that is already influencing the operation of the power system.
Underlying electricity demand across the NEM reached a record June-quarter high despite above-average temperatures reducing heating requirements, with growing electrification, industrial activity and data centre loads offsetting the weather-driven decline.
Operational demand also increased during daylight hours as electricity consumed by battery charging, industrial users and data centre loads outpaced the growth in rooftop solar generation, marking a significant shift in electricity consumption patterns. The impact is becoming increasingly visible at state level.
In NSW, average electricity demand from data centres climbed 35 per cent over the past year to 451 megawatts. In Victoria, average demand almost doubled from 104MW to 204MW, helping make Victoria the only mainland state to record higher operational electricity demand during the June quarter despite milder weather reducing heating demand.
The report also provides one of the clearest snapshots yet of the scale of new AI-related infrastructure seeking to connect to Australia’s electricity grid.
By the end of June, AEMO was tracking 17 proposed data centre developments progressing through the transmission connection process with a combined maximum connection capacity of 9GW.
More than half of that capacity is in NSW, while Victoria accounts for 31 per cent and South Australia the remaining 17 per cent. Twelve projects representing 7.6GW remain in the application stage, while five projects totalling 1.4GW are progressing through implementation. The figures highlight the balancing act confronting the Albanese government as it seeks to capitalise on the economic opportunities presented by artificial intelligence while ensuring the additional electricity demand does not place upward pressure on power prices for households and businesses.
